steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on personalized abstractive summarization with a three-part pipeline (generator, instructor, editor) built around ChatGPT. Motivate why LLM outputs need to be tailored to user preferences, explain the pipeline, and briefly summarize the experiments.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Large language models and their success in NLP
2. The problem: outputs don't match user preferences; editing vs one-time generation
3. Our generator / instructor / editor decomposition
4. Task, datasets and main findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Large language models
- e.g. InstructGPT, ChatGPT; essential resources in NLP
- proficient across broad range of tasks: machine translation, question answering, text summarization
- potential to drive innovation in language-based technologies -> growing enthusiasm in research community

2. Tailoring outputs to users
- despite impressive generation quality, hard to tailor outputs to user's preference
- outputs don't consistently satisfy users' preferences/expectations
- prevalent fix: carefully crafted prompts to steer models
- but: one-time left-to-right generation vs humans' iterative refinement and editing
- prior works: generate-and-edit better than one-time generation, even with single editing iteration
- -> this paper: integrate LLMs (ChatGPT) into automatic iterative editing pipeline

3. Method
- prior approach: generator + corrector; ours: generator, instructor, editor (Figure 1)
- inference-only large models for complex tasks (content generation, correction); smaller models for simpler task (user-specific editing instructions)
- instructor: targeted directives for editing/refining generator's initial outputs
- initialized by training on human-authored (oracle) instructions, obtainable from history of user's behaviour
- then fine-tuned with editor-steered reinforcement learning; reward = degree edited output aligns with user preferences -> better compatibility with editor

4. Experiments
- task: text summarization (concise, informative summary for given document(s))
- datasets: DeFacto, CNNDM; preferences: factual consistency, coverage
- ChatGPT = generator and editor
- with small instructor's instructions, edited output better aligned with user preference on both datasets
- iterative editing: more iterations -> output better meets user's needs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models such as InstructGPT and ChatGPT have become essential resources in natural language processing (NLP). These models are very good at a broad range of NLP tasks, like machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. Since they could drive more innovation in language-based technologies, the research community has become more and more interested in exploring and advancing large language models.

But even though these models generate text of impressive quality, it is still a problem to tailor their outputs to what the user prefers. In several scenarios people have observed that the outputs of language models do not always satisfy what users prefer or expect. A common way to deal with this is to carefully craft prompts so that the models produce outputs that fit better with what the users want. However, as existing research notes, language models generate their output once from left to right, which is different from the way humans usually refine and edit their text iteratively. Also, prior works have shown that a generate-and-edit process works better than one-time generation, even when there is only one editing iteration. Because of these findings, in this paper we look at putting large language models (ChatGPT) into an automatic iterative editing pipeline.

3. Method
- prior approach: generator + corrector; ours: generator, instructor, editor (Figure 1)
- large inference-only models for generation and correction; smaller model for user-specific editing instructions
- instructor gives targeted directives to edit/refine the generator's initial outputs
- trained first on human-authored (oracle) instructions, which can come from the history of user's behaviour
- then fine-tuned with editor-steered RL; reward = how well edited output aligns with user preferences -> more compatible with editor

4. Experiments
- text summarization: concise and informative summary for the given document(s)
- DeFacto and CNNDM; preferences on factual consistency and coverage
- ChatGPT as generator and editor
- instructor's instructions -> edited output better aligned with preference on both datasets
- more editing iterations -> output better meets user's needs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models such as InstructGPT and ChatGPT have become essential resources in natural language processing (NLP). These models are very good at a broad range of NLP tasks, like machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. Since they could drive more innovation in language-based technologies, the research community has become more and more interested in exploring and advancing large language models.

But even though these models generate text of impressive quality, it is still a problem to tailor their outputs to what the user prefers. In several scenarios people have observed that the outputs of language models do not always satisfy what users prefer or expect. A common way to deal with this is to carefully craft prompts so that the models produce outputs that fit better with what the users want. However, as existing research notes, language models generate their output once from left to right, which is different from the way humans usually refine and edit their text iteratively. Also, prior works have shown that a generate-and-edit process works better than one-time generation, even when there is only one editing iteration. Because of these findings, in this paper we look at putting large language models (ChatGPT) into an automatic iterative editing pipeline.

Unlike the approach of prior work, which splits the generation process into a generator and a corrector, we split it into three components: a generator, an instructor, and an editor (see Figure 1). With this structure we can use inference-only large models for the complex tasks of generating and correcting content, and use smaller models for the simpler task of generating editing instructions that are specific to the user. The instructor gives targeted directives for editing and refining the initial outputs of the generator. It is first trained on human-authored, or oracle, instructions, which can be obtained from the history of the user's behaviour. After this, the model is fine-tuned with editor-steered reinforcement learning, where the reward function directly measures how much the output edited by the editor aligns with user preferences. This makes the model more compatible with the editor.

We pick text summarization as the task for evaluating this new framework. The task is to generate a concise and informative summary for the given document(s). In this paper we run experiments on two summarization datasets (DeFacto and CNNDM), and we focus on user preferences related to factual consistency and coverage. ChatGPT is used as the generator and also as the editor model. The experiments show that with the instructions generated by the small instructor model, the edited output is better aligned with what the user prefers on both datasets. More experiments on iterative editing show that the output can meet the user's needs better when there are more iterations of editing.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models, such as InstructGPT [1] and ChatGPT, have emerged as essential resources in the field of natural language processing (NLP). These models have shown a high level of proficiency across a broad range of NLP tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. Given their potential to drive further innovation in language-based technologies, the research community has shown growing enthusiasm for exploring and advancing large language models.

However, despite the impressive generation quality of these models, a persistent challenge is tailoring their outputs to meet the user's preference [3]. In several scenarios, it has been observed that the outputs of language models do not consistently satisfy users' preferences or expectations [4]. A common approach to addressing this limitation is to carefully craft prompts that steer the models toward outputs that better align with users' objectives. Nonetheless, as noted in existing research [5], the one-time left-to-right generation process of language models contrasts with the iterative refinement and editing that humans commonly employ. Furthermore, prior works [6,7] have demonstrated that the generate-and-edit process is more effective than one-time generation, even with a single editing iteration. Motivated by these findings, this paper explores integrating large language models (ChatGPT) into an automatic iterative editing pipeline.

In contrast to the approach taken by [2], which decomposes the generation process into a generator and a corrector, our method decomposes it into three components: a generator, an instructor, and an editor (refer to Figure 1). This structure allows us to leverage inference-only large models for the complex tasks of content generation and correction, while using smaller models for the simpler task of generating user-specific editing instructions. The instructor is designed to provide targeted directives for editing and refining the initial outputs of the generator. It is initialized by training on human-authored, or oracle, instructions, which can be obtained from the history of the user's behaviour. The model is then fine-tuned through editor-steered reinforcement learning, where the reward function directly quantifies how well the output edited by the editor aligns with user preferences, which enhances the model's compatibility with the editor.

We choose text summarization, the task of generating a concise and informative summary for the given document(s), as the focal task for evaluating this framework. We conduct experimental evaluations on two summarization datasets (DeFacto [3] and CNNDM [8]), focusing on user preferences related to factual consistency and coverage, and employ ChatGPT as both the generator and the editor model. Our experiments indicate that with the instructions generated by the small instructor model, the edited output is better aligned with the user's preference on both datasets. Further experiments on iterative editing show that the output can better meet the user's needs with more iterations of editing.
